module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1056

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1056](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1056)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Nat
namespace Erdos1056

/--
The proposition that the modular product of a collection of consecutive interval equals $1$ modulo $p$,
where intervals are defined by a function specifying the consecutive boundaries.
-/
def AllModProdEqualsOne (p : ℕ) {k : ℕ} (boundaries : Fin (k + 1) → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i : Fin k,
    (∏ n ∈ Finset.Ico (boundaries i.castSucc) (boundaries (i.castSucc + 1)), n) ≡ 1 [MOD p]

/--
Let $k ≥ 2$. Does there exist a prime $p$ and consecutive intervals $I_0,\dots,I_k$
such that $\prod\limits_{n{\in}I_i}n \equiv 1 \mod n$ for all $1 \le i \le k$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1056 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ k ≥ 2, ∃ (p : ℕ) (_ : p.Prime) (boundaries : Fin (k + 1) → ℕ) (_ : StrictMono boundaries),
    AllModProdEqualsOne p boundaries := by
  sorry

/--
This is problem A15 in Guy's collection [Gu04], where he reports that in a letter in 1979
Erdős observed that $3 * 4 \equiv 5 * 6 * 7 \equiv 1 \mod 11$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1056.variants.k2 :
    AllModProdEqualsOne 11 ![3, 5, 8] := by
  unfold AllModProdEqualsOne
  decide

/--
Makowski [Ma83] found, for $k=3$:
$2 * 3 * 4 * 5 \equiv 6 * 7 * 8 * 9 * 10 * 11 \equiv 12 * 13 * 14 * 15 \equiv 1 \mod 17$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1056.variants.k3 :
    AllModProdEqualsOne 17 ![2, 6, 12, 16] := by
  unfold AllModProdEqualsOne
  decide

/--
Noll and Simmons asked, more generally, whether there are solutions to
$q_1! \equiv \dots \equiv q_k! \mod p$ for arbitrarily large $k$ (with $q_1 < \dots < q_k$).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1056.variants.noll_simmons :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᶠ k in Filter.atTop,
    ∃ (p : ℕ) (_ : p.Prime) (Q : Fin k → ℕ) (_ : StrictMono Q) (_ : ∀ i, Q i < p),
    ∀ i j : Fin k, (Q i)! ≡ (Q j)! [MOD p] := by
  sorry

end Erdos1056

findings.description: The docstring at line 41 writes the congruence modulo n, where n is the product's dummy variable, instead of modulo the prime p. The Lean statement correctly uses AllModProdEqualsOne p, so the formal mathematics is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős Problem 1056 explicitly asks for consecutive intervals whose products satisfy ∏_{n∈I_i} n ≡ 1 (mod p). Read at https://web.archive.org/web/20260709213210/https://www.erdosproblems.com/1056 .
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `\mod n` with `\pmod{p}` in the docstring. For consistency with the same source sentence, write the interval list as `I_1,\dots,I_k`.

reformulations.difference: The source asks for solutions for arbitrarily large k, whereas Lean requires solutions for all sufficiently large k using ∀ᶠ k in Filter.atTop.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The existence predicate is downward closed in k: restrict an increasing solution Q : Fin m → ℕ to its first k entries whenever k ≤ m. Thus arbitrarily large solutions imply solutions for every k, hence eventually every k. Conversely, eventual existence on ℕ immediately gives arbitrarily large solutions. This equivalence was proved as NS_eventually_iff_arbitrarily_large in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, without using the sorry-backed conjectures.

sources_consulted: Richard K. Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory (2004), A15, p. 54; Google Books indexed excerpts for A15 and Noll: https://books.google.com/books?id=1AP2CEGxTkgC&jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=A15 and https://books.google.com/books?id=1AP2CEGxTkgC&jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=Noll
Carlos Rivera, PrimePuzzles Problem 27, including Jens Kruse Andersen's explanation: https://www.primepuzzles.net/problems/prob_027.htm
Checked-out Mathlib definitions and lemmas for Nat.ModEq, Nat.factorial, Nat.Prime, Fin arithmetic, StrictMono, natural-number Finset intervals, and Filter.atTop; FormalConjecturesUtil/Answer.lean.
review.notes: Checked all five declarations. Scratch checks verify that i.castSucc + 1 equals i.succ (no wraparound), StrictMono makes every interval nonempty, and no admissible interval contains a multiple of p. Both numerical examples were independently checked. The factorial bound Q i < p expresses nonzero factorial residues, consistent with Andersen's explanation; Noll's own table explicitly permits index 0. No substantive mathematical mismatch was found. The live Erdős page was blocked, so its archived statement was used; the current source database still records the problem as open. Guy was accessible only through indexed excerpts, and the original Ma83 article was unavailable, but the cited page states both numerical examples explicitly. Final scratch compilation had zero errors or warnings; the reviewed file was not modified.
